art.alt: An engraved relay machine transforms through neural layers into attention geometry.
art.prompt:
Use case: stylized-concept
Asset type: wide 16:9 editorial series plate for a serious long-form knowledge garden
Primary request: depict the history of artificial intelligence as one continuous archival mechanism transforming across time: on the left, hand-built relay logic, punched cards, early symbolic diagrams and a cybernetic feedback governor; through the middle, layered perceptron meshes, laboratory traces and a restrained neural lattice; on the right, the same mechanism resolves into elegant transformer-like attention geometry and modular machine intelligence. The transformation should feel archaeological and causal, not celebratory or futuristic.
Scene/backdrop: warm cream rag paper, horizontal museum-table composition with faint chronological strata and translucent technical overlays
Subject: an evolving cybernetic machine/relay lineage, physically continuous from early mechanical and symbolic forms into neural and transformer geometry
Style/medium: original tactile printmaking, copperplate engraving and woodcut linework combined with translucent technical drafting layers, serious literary-scientific editorial illustration
Composition/framing: cinematic wide 16:9, left-to-right transformation, dense but legible, strong central rhythm, generous breathing space at edges; no framed panels
Lighting/mood: quiet archival gravity, intellectual wonder, precise rather than dramatic
Color palette: cream paper, charcoal black, oxide red, with one restrained ultramarine accent
Materials/textures: visible paper grain, dry ink, etched hatching, subtle registration offsets, translucent vellum-like overlays
Constraints: textless; no letters, numbers, captions, logos, interface UI, or watermark; historically suggestive without portraying identifiable people; coherent single illustration
Avoid: generic sci-fi, neon, glowing robot heads, humanoid robots, floating dashboards, stock circuit-board imagery, glossy 3D rendering, named-artist imitation

visuals.title: The ingredients accumulated while the headline field froze
visuals.caption: The apparent winter from 1986 to 2012 concealed the four lines of work that made the deep-learning break possible.

items.label: Backpropagation
items.detail: Multi-layer networks could learn hidden representations by propagating error backward.

items.label: Statistical turn
items.detail: Probability and data-estimated parameters displaced brittle hand-written rule bases.

items.label: Closed-world search
items.detail: Deep Blue showed symbolic search at full strength—and the limits of a system that learned nothing.

items.label: GPU compute
items.detail: Graphics processors made the matrix arithmetic of deep networks economically tractable.

items.label: Training craft
items.detail: Better activations, regularization, and initialization made deep networks trainable in practice.

items.label: Shared data
items.detail: ImageNet supplied more than a million labeled examples and a public arena for comparison.

visuals.title: Why XOR defeated one line and yielded to two intermediate ideas
visuals.caption: A single perceptron cannot separate XOR, while two hidden units re-express it as OR minus AND.

items.label: Single boundary
items.detail: The four XOR inequalities contradict one another; no weights w₁, w₂, b satisfy all four.

items.label: Hidden OR
items.detail: The first intermediate unit fires when at least one input is on.

items.label: Hidden AND
items.detail: The second intermediate unit fires only when both inputs are on.

items.label: OR, not AND
items.detail: The output combines h₁ and h₂ to return 0, 1, 1, 0 exactly.

visuals.title: The first winter exposed different limits that looked like one failure
visuals.caption: A correct theorem about one architecture and a correct audit of toy-world scaling converged on the same funding collapse, while the missing compute-and-data diagnosis remained largely unseen.

items.label: Perceptron argument
items.detail: Minsky and Papert proved that a single-layer perceptron cannot compute XOR.

items.label: Training gap
items.detail: Multi-layer networks could represent XOR, but no practical training method was then available.

items.label: Lighthill audit
items.detail: Toy demonstrations failed to justify their promises once real search spaces and real funding were examined.

items.label: Search explosion
items.detail: Methods that worked in tiny formal worlds drowned as the number of possible states grew.

items.label: Commonsense gap
items.detail: Real environments required background knowledge that people rarely state and engineers could not exhaustively encode.

items.label: Hidden diagnosis
items.detail: Connectionism also lacked the compute and data it would later need, but almost nobody named those as the bottleneck.

visuals.title: Each AI body plan metabolized the resource its era made abundant
visuals.caption: The field's succession reads less like a planned ladder than a sequence of organisms selected by changing constraints.

items.label: Symbolic
items.detail: Scarce compute and data favored compressing available human expertise into rules.

items.label: Statistical
items.detail: Digitized corpora favored methods that could learn from counting instead of hand-written grammar.

items.label: Neural
items.detail: GPU compute and labeled data rewarded architectures that parallelized and learned features.

items.label: Foundation
items.detail: Capital and web-scale data favored one generalist pretrained according to scaling laws.

items.label: Agents
items.detail: The scarce resource became reliable verification as systems moved from answers to completed tasks.

visuals.title: Machine translation as a lineage of changing bottlenecks
visuals.caption: The same ambiguous sentence exposes what each successive paradigm could metabolize—and what killed it.

items.label: Rules
items.detail: A symbolic translator cannot disambiguate “spirit” without unwritable world knowledge.

items.label: Phrase counts
items.detail: Parallel text resolves familiar phrases but produces stilted output when counting hits its ceiling.

items.label: Neural sequence
items.detail: Whole-sentence fluency jumps, but the model remains a translation specialist.

items.label: General model
items.detail: One system translates, explains the idiom, and checks its own result with tools.

visuals.title: Symbolic AI first fit its environment, then lost the environment
visuals.caption: The paradigm's rise and extinction follow a resource chain: spend abundant expert labor to conserve scarce compute, until both its internal ceiling and its hardware niche break.

items.label: Resource climate
items.detail: Compute was scarce, digitized data barely existed, and human expertise was comparatively available.

items.label: Adaptive strategy
items.detail: Engineers compressed expertise into explicit rules so machines could reason without costly learning.

items.label: Commercial bloom
items.detail: Expert systems such as XCON delivered real value and supported a specialized Lisp-machine industry.

items.label: Internal ceiling
items.detail: Thousands of interacting rules became brittle, while tacit skills resisted being written down at all.

items.label: External shock
items.detail: General-purpose workstations erased the economic reason for dedicated Lisp hardware.

items.label: Selection outcome
items.detail: The lineage lost its budget and funding climate rather than being defeated by elegance alone.

visuals.title: The scenarios differ by observable hinges, not mood
visuals.caption: Each future is a chain of assumptions with evidence that could confirm it and evidence that could kill it.

items.label: Fast takeoff
items.detail: Requires recent time-horizon doubling to hold, AI to accelerate AI research, and deployment friction to fall.

items.label: Steady compounding
items.detail: Requires long-run capability growth, organizational diffusion, and infrastructure financed by real revenue.

items.label: Plateau and diffusion
items.detail: Requires inference-time scaling to exhaust its overhang with no new capability axis.

visuals.title: One target, three trend windows, three arrival dates
visuals.caption: Moving from a 320-minute horizon to 9,600 minutes takes about five doublings, but the chosen window moves the answer by more than a year.

items.label: Start
items.detail: The worked example begins from Claude Opus 4.5's roughly 320-minute measured horizon.

items.label: Recent window
items.detail: Five doublings at 89 days each place the month-scale horizon around mid-2027.

items.label: Post-2023 window
items.detail: Five doublings at 131 days each place it around late 2027.

items.label: All-time window
items.detail: Five doublings at about 196 days each place it around late 2028.

items.label: Uncertainty band
items.detail: The stated 170–729 minute interval shifts every date by roughly one doubling.

visuals.title: A future claim earns weight by carrying its date, assumptions, and type
visuals.caption: The room replaces one confident prediction with a protocol that lets you see exactly what changed when evidence moves.

items.label: Start with the miss record
items.detail: Famous experts underestimated and overestimated progress, so confidence and access are not evidence.

items.label: Date the evidence
items.detail: Every empirical signal is tied to August 2026 because an undated frontier claim hides its decay.

items.label: Name the assumptions
items.detail: A scenario states the hinges that must hold instead of presenting its outcome as a forecasted fact.

items.label: Type the claim
items.detail: Measurement, contest, and speculation keep different grammar so their authority cannot silently merge.

items.label: Watch the hinge
items.detail: When an assumption breaks, update the scenario rather than defending the date attached to it.

visuals.title: The 2026 model landscape is an ecosystem, not one leaderboard
visuals.caption: The room maps closed labs, open-weight challengers, context, price, and access as separate dimensions that expire at different speeds.

items.label: Closed frontier
items.detail: Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI, and Meta compete through hosted models, with Meta straddling the weight boundary.

items.label: Open-weight challengers
items.detail: DeepSeek, Moonshot, Zhipu, and Alibaba put downloadable or promised weights near the frontier.

items.label: Context
items.detail: Published windows range from Grok's 500K to Gemini Pro's 2M in the dated table.

items.label: Price
items.detail: Headline token rates conceal threshold billing, output premiums, and retries per completed task.

items.label: Access
items.detail: A model can be technically available yet restricted by government action, region, license, or nationality controls.

visuals.title: Per-token prices become concrete only when attached to a workload
visuals.caption: For 400K input and 30K output tokens, the room's dated arithmetic produces three very different bills before retries or quality enter.

items.label: Claude Opus 5
items.detail: $2.00 of input plus $0.75 of output under the flat listed rates.

items.label: Grok 4.6
items.detail: Crossing the 200K prompt threshold moves the entire request to the higher price band.

items.label: DeepSeek V4-Pro
items.detail: The dated off-peak rates yield the lowest token bill in the comparison.

items.label: Completed-task cost
items.detail: Three attempts or triple the output can erase a model's nominal per-token advantage.

visuals.title: A model became a controlled dependency overnight
visuals.caption: The Fable 5 episode turned policy risk from an abstract footnote into a dated failure mode for anyone building on a frontier API.

items.label: Launch
items.detail: Anthropic releases Fable 5 and Mythos 5.

items.label: Global suspension
items.detail: Immediate export controls force both models offline because nationality cannot be verified in real time.

items.label: Public challenge
items.detail: Security researchers ask Commerce to reverse the restriction.

items.label: Narrow restoration
items.detail: Mythos 5 returns for a vetted set of U.S. organizations while broader controls remain.

items.label: Controls lifted
items.detail: Commerce reviews new mitigations and removes the restriction.

items.label: Global return
items.detail: Access resumes worldwide, leaving the dependency lesson intact.

visuals.title: A benchmark's predictable life from lighthouse to trophy
visuals.caption: Shared tests accelerate progress, then lose epistemic value as scores climb, incentives concentrate, and proxy and target separate.

items.label: Launch hard
items.detail: A fresh dataset, metric, and protocol expose a capability frontier models cannot yet cross.

items.label: Coordinate
items.detail: A public leaderboard focuses thousands of researchers on one legible objective.

items.label: Climb
items.detail: Training and methods adapt to the shared test, compressing years of progress into months.

items.label: Saturate
items.detail: Scores bunch near the ceiling and remaining differences stop carrying their old meaning.

items.label: Replace
items.detail: The old test remains as a trophy while a harder benchmark becomes the new lighthouse.

visuals.title: Goodhart's law does not need a villain
visuals.caption: Once the score becomes a target, five distinct mechanisms can inflate it without improving the capability its name implies.

items.label: Contamination
items.detail: Test items leak through the internet into pretraining, turning evaluation partly into memory.

items.label: Teaching to the test
items.detail: Labs train hardest on the domains that dominate public comparisons.

items.label: Leaderboard gaming
items.detail: A tuned or non-public variant can be submitted instead of the model users actually receive.

items.label: Owning the yardstick
items.detail: Funding or privileged access changes the public meaning of an otherwise legitimate score.

items.label: Broken answer key
items.detail: A model can be rewarded for reproducing an official answer contradicted by evidence.

visuals.title: Turn one benchmark score back into an auditable claim
visuals.caption: The room's four-step method converts a bare 55% into a test definition, an uncertainty range, a protocol-specific result, and inspectable items.

items.label: Identify the test
items.detail: Establish the 2,500 closed-ended questions, subject coverage, and expert reference before reading the score.

items.label: Estimate key defects
items.detail: Carry the audited bio-and-chem error range forward instead of treating every official answer as ground truth.

items.label: State the assumption
items.detail: The worked example uses a conservative illustrative 15% whole-exam defect rate rather than presenting it as measured.

items.label: Read the protocol
items.detail: The same model can move sharply when tools are allowed, so model, scaffold, and rules belong with the score.

items.label: Inspect the items
items.detail: Reading even ten open questions can expose ambiguous wording or a visibly wrong answer key.

items.label: Reframe the number
items.detail: The result becomes a bounded claim about one instrument, not a free-floating percentage of intelligence.

visuals.title: Feedback became a science by turning correction into an object of study
visuals.caption: A mechanical governor became a stability problem, then a general language for control and communication.

items.label: Centrifugal governor
items.detail: A spinning mechanism throttles a steam engine as its speed departs from the target.

items.label: Stability mathematics
items.detail: Maxwell turns governor behavior into a formal problem of oscillation and control.

items.label: Cybernetics
items.detail: Control and communication in animals and machines become one named research program.

visuals.title: Ashby's law as a three-move game
visuals.caption: A regulator can collapse three disturbances to one outcome only when it can distinguish and answer all three.

items.label: World variety
items.detail: The disturbance can choose among three distinct moves.

items.label: Matched regulator
items.detail: With three countermoves, the regulator maps every disturbance to outcome a.

items.label: Amputated regulator
items.detail: With only two countermoves, the third disturbance has no answer that yields a.

items.label: Residual variety
items.detail: The outcome set must contain at least two values; wiring cleverness cannot evade the count.

visuals.title: The 1956 secession changed the object of study, but feedback returned
visuals.caption: Cybernetics, symbolic AI, and modern machine learning each center a different object, mathematics, and test of success; today's missing guarantees reveal what the split left behind.

items.label: Cybernetics
items.detail: Feedback loops regulate continuous systems through stability, information, and error correction.

items.label: Symbolic AI
items.detail: Discrete representations support logic, search, planning, and theorem proving.

items.label: Modern ML
items.detail: Differentiable functions learn from data through statistics, linear algebra, and optimization.

items.label: The returning inheritance
items.detail: Training and deployed agents are feedback loops even when they no longer use the cybernetic name.

items.label: The unresolved debt
items.detail: Modern learning is powerful but weak on closed-loop stability and safe-operating guarantees.

visuals.title: Modern AI grew by passing a small set of ideas forward
visuals.caption: The list is less a cabinet of isolated breakthroughs than a relay of computation, error, scale, and feedback.

items.label: Neurons compute
items.detail: Threshold units, behavioral tests, and trainable perceptrons establish the substrate and the learning bet.

items.label: Error teaches
items.detail: Backpropagation, gated memory, and convolution make hidden representations trainable and useful.

items.label: Scale breaks through
items.detail: GPUs, learned features, attention, residuals, reward, and search trigger the deep-learning explosion.

items.label: Attention scales
items.detail: Transformers, pretraining, scaling laws, in-context learning, science, and human feedback define the new regime.

visuals.title: A token asks, scores, normalizes, and mixes
visuals.caption: The room's two-dimensional example reduces the transformer's core operation to a calculation you can verify on paper.

items.label: Query and keys
items.detail: Token A asks with q=[1,0] against keys [2,0] and [0,2].

items.label: Scaled scores
items.detail: Dot products divided by √2 produce approximately 1.41 and 0.

items.label: Softmax weights
items.detail: The scores become a normalized allocation of roughly 0.80 and 0.20.

items.label: Value mixture
items.detail: Applying those weights to [10,0] and [0,10] yields [8,2].

visuals.title: The deep-learning explosion was a relay of removed constraints
visuals.caption: From vision through control, each landmark inherited the previous machinery and removed one practical obstruction to scale, context, depth, or action.

items.label: Learn the features
items.detail: AlexNet scales convolution on GPUs and replaces hand-designed vision features with learned ones.

items.label: Geometrize meaning
items.detail: Word2vec makes semantic relationships visible as structure in learned vectors.

items.label: Learn whole sequences
items.detail: Encoder-decoder LSTMs turn translation into one end-to-end model but squeeze the input through one vector.

items.label: Open the bottleneck
items.detail: Attention lets each output step look back across all input positions instead of trusting one compressed summary.

items.label: Make depth trainable
items.detail: Residual shortcuts ask layers for corrections to identity, allowing 152-layer networks to optimize cleanly.

items.label: Close perception into action
items.detail: DQN closes perception into reward-guided action; AlphaGo adds tree search to learned policy and value networks.

visuals.title: The machine-learning canon advances by exposing its predecessor's limit
visuals.caption: Across the twenty papers, formal guarantees, practical architectures, and empirical counterexamples repeatedly trade the lead.

items.label: Learning formalized
items.detail: SGD, perceptrons, VC dimension, and PAC learning turn adaptation into a mathematical object.

items.label: Connectionist toolkit
items.detail: Backpropagation, convolution, margin methods, LSTMs, boosting, and forests become reusable workhorses.

items.label: Deep eruption
items.detail: Pretraining, GPUs, generative models, dropout, Adam, and residual paths make depth practical.

items.label: Architectural border
items.detail: The transformer removes recurrence and unlocks parallel sequence learning.

items.label: Theory reckons
items.detail: Random-label memorization and double descent show why classical capacity stories are incomplete.

visuals.title: The perceptron learns OR by keeping only corrections
visuals.caption: Four mistakes move the weight vector from zero to a boundary that classifies all four OR inputs correctly.

items.label: Begin
items.detail: Weights start at (0,0,0); a zero dot product predicts −1.

items.label: First positive
items.detail: The mistaken (0,1) example adds its vector, producing weights (1,0,1).

items.label: Repair the zero
items.detail: The false positive on (0,0) subtracts the bias input and later corrections add x₁.

items.label: Converge
items.detail: Final weights (0,1,1) give dot products 0,1,1,2 and the labels −1,+1,+1,+1.

items.label: XOR test
items.detail: Changing only the labels to XOR prevents convergence because no single line separates the cases.

visuals.title: Memorization broke the old capacity story without explaining the new one
visuals.caption: The 2017 and 2019 papers show that models able to fit pure noise can still generalize, and that test error can fall again after the interpolation threshold.

items.label: Classical expectation
items.detail: As model capacity grows past the useful fit, test error should eventually rise in a familiar U-shaped tradeoff.

items.label: Random-label test
items.detail: Standard deep networks fit completely random training labels with the same architecture and optimizer.

items.label: Capacity bound fails
items.detail: A class expressive enough to memorize noise cannot be explained by simple worst-case capacity alone.

items.label: Interpolation spike
items.detail: Test error peaks near the point where the model just fits every training example.

items.label: Second descent
items.detail: Increase capacity further and test error can fall again, making overparameterization part of the working regime.

items.label: Open mechanism
items.detail: Data structure, architecture, and optimizer bias must matter together, but no accepted general theory closes the account.
